candidates.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
candidates.proposition: The standard critical Greek text indicates that the autographic wording survives among the manuscript readings in virtually every disputed place.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted argument continues Wallace's identified presentation and uses his affirmative position on textual recoverability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This converts the critical edition's treatment of conjectural readings into direct support for the claim that the original wording remains recoverable from extant witnesses.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's contention that early corruption prevents confidence that surviving readings preserve the autographic wording.

candidates.contextSummary: Wallace describes the critical text and its apparatus, contrasts many listed variants with very few proposed conjectures, and argues that an original reading is ordinarily represented among the available alternatives.

candidates.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
candidates.proposition: New Testament scholarship, including Ehrman's own authorship arguments, routinely presupposes reliable knowledge of the wording in nearly every relevant passage.
candidates.attributionBasis: Wallace explicitly discusses Ehrman and Ehrman's publications from the standpoint of the affirmative debater's ongoing presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move alleges a practical inconsistency between denying recoverability and conducting detailed scholarship that depends on stable wording across multiple New Testament books.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's denial that scholars can know whether the reconstructed text corresponds to the authors' original wording.

candidates.contextSummary: Wallace invokes the scholarly consensus and then uses Ehrman's vocabulary-based analysis of disputed Pauline letters as an example of research that requires dependable access to the relevant wording.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Wallace's presentation does not supply evidence establishing that surviving witnesses preserve the original wording, and Ehrman's older statements do not resolve that problem.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the response to Ehrman, who addresses Wallace by name and describes his own changed position in the first person.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This identifies the con side's governing objection to Wallace's case: evidence from surviving witnesses cannot by itself establish what happened before those witnesses existed.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wallace's appeal to Ehrman's earlier publications as evidence that even Ehrman presupposes recovery of the original text.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman notes substantial agreement but says Wallace has not reached the central epistemic issue, rejects reliance on older books because his view changed, and renews the demand for supporting evidence.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: The small proportion of meaningful and viable surviving variants does not address potentially significant changes introduced before the earliest surviving manuscripts.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Ehrman's announced response and directly challenges a numerical claim attributed to Wallace's preceding presentation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It distinguishes the measurable variation in extant evidence from the unobservable transmission period, blocking a principal quantitative argument for confidence in the text.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wallace's argument that only a very small percentage of the numerous surviving variants are both meaningful and viable.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman provisionally accepts Wallace's percentage but argues that it concerns only surviving variants, then asks how anyone could count omissions, editions, or alterations predating extant witnesses.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: A textual difference can be historically significant even when it changes no essential Christian doctrine, so doctrinal stability is not an adequate measure of textual significance.
candidates.attributionBasis: Ehrman's response explicitly grants the theological point attributed to Wallace and then supplies his own counterexample and criterion of significance.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This rebuts a major trust argument by separating theological consequences from historical and textual importance, preserving the relevance of substantial variants.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wallace's reassurance that no essential Christian belief is affected by any viable textual variant in the manuscripts.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman accepts that variants may leave doctrine unchanged but uses the hypothetical disappearance of several whole books to show that losses can remain extremely important without altering a creed.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Confidence in the New Testament requires an evidential basis for believing that the earliest surviving copies descend from accurate rather than seriously altered predecessors.
candidates.attributionBasis: Ehrman closes his response by directly requesting that Wallace answer a repeated question about the ancestry of the earliest copies.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states the core con challenge linking unavailable pre-survival transmission evidence directly to whether the text can responsibly be trusted.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wallace's conclusion that the original New Testament wording is recoverable with relative confidence from the accumulated evidence.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman asks how Wallace knows significant alteration did not occur before extant witnesses, sharpens the issue to whether early copies had accurate exemplars, and connects inability to answer with trust.

candidates.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
candidates.proposition: Early circulation, repeated copying, independent versions, and patristic witnesses provide cumulative probabilistic evidence against a sparse and unrecoverable initial transmission.
candidates.attributionBasis: After the moderator names Wallace, the speaker addresses Ehrman's scenario and advances the affirmative side's explicitly probabilistic answer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Wallace's principal evidential response to the missing-first-copies objection by arguing that early branching created multiple independent lines of textual control.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's claim that nothing establishes whether the first copies were accurate or how much alteration preceded surviving manuscripts.

candidates.contextSummary: Wallace cites circulation of Pauline letters, use of Mark by Matthew and Luke, repeated reading and copying, comparison with classical works, early versions, and patristic material as converging evidence.

candidates.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
candidates.proposition: Although hard proof about the earliest copies is unavailable, substantial indirect evidence makes it probable that the extant text preserves what the New Testament authors wrote in essential respects.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator returns the floor to Wallace, who addresses Ehrman and states the affirmative conclusion in the first-person debate exchange.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move expressly defines the affirmative standard as warranted probability rather than certainty and applies it directly to essential textual recoverability.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's repeated demand for hard evidence proving that pre-survival copies were accurate and free from significant alteration.

candidates.contextSummary: Wallace concedes that neither side possesses hard evidence about the missing period but maintains that the accumulated indirect evidence supports confidence in essential continuity with the authors' writings.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Contemporary textual criticism can reconstruct the earliest text from which surviving witnesses descend without establishing that this reconstructed initial text is the author's original.
candidates.attributionBasis: An audience question is followed by Ehrman's direct disagreement with Wallace and his description of current textual-critical terminology and aims.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This draws the decisive con distinction between attainable reconstruction and autographic identification, directly limiting what textual criticism can warrant about the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Wallace's claim that most scholars believe the original New Testament wording has been substantially recovered.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman says major scholarly centers avoid the language of original text and instead reconstruct the ancestral text behind surviving witnesses, whose identity with the autograph remains unknown.

candidates.speaker: Daniel B. Wallace
candidates.proposition: The relevant scholarly consensus is that the New Testament has been largely recovered in essentials, even if textual critics qualify the terminology used for the original text.
candidates.attributionBasis: Wallace explicitly corrects what he says he did not claim and restates his position about New Testament scholars and recoverability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This preserves the affirmative conclusion by distinguishing terminological caution among specialist textual critics from the broader scholarly practice of relying on an essentially recovered text.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's argument that specialists' abandonment of the term original text undermines Wallace's appeal to scholarly consensus.

candidates.contextSummary: Wallace clarifies that his claim concerned New Testament scholars rather than every textual critic, appeals to ordinary scholarly analysis as evidence, and asserts recovery in essentials even for corrupt witnesses.
